title: Divide 72 by the interest rate to see roughly when money doubles
body: Money earning compound interest doubles in roughly 72 ÷ (the yearly rate in %) years: at 6% that is 12 years, at 9% about 8. It works because each year’s interest earns interest too, so the money is multiplied by the same factor every year, and the exact doubling time, ln 2 ÷ ln(1 + rate), comes out close to 72 ÷ rate for everyday rates. The rule appears in Luca Pacioli’s *Summa de arithmetica* of 1494, given without explanation, so it is thought to be even older.

slides.question: At 8% interest a year, added once a year, roughly how many years does it take money to double?
slides.explanation: About 9. The rule of 72 gives 72 ÷ 8 = 9, and the exact answer for yearly compounding is 9.01 years.

slides.alt: Animation on green ledger paper: a stack of gold coins grows as a 6% ledger adds interest year by year until it doubles in year 12. Curves for 3%, 6% and 9% cross the doubling line near 72 ÷ rate, 72 coins regroup into 8 × 9, 6 × 12, 4 × 18, 3 × 24 and 2 × 36, and Pacioli’s 1494 book appears.

slides.heading: Why it works
slides.text: With compound interest, each year’s interest joins the balance, so next year’s interest is a little bigger. The money is multiplied by (1 + rate) every year, and doubling takes ln 2 ÷ ln(1 + rate) years, which is close to 72 divided by the rate in percent.

slides.heading: Exact years to double, at yearly compounding
slides.note: The rule of 72 says 24, 12, 8 and 6 years.

slides.heading: Why 72 and not 69?
slides.text: When interest is added continuously, 69.3 is more accurate, because ln 2 is about 0.693. But 72 is close for everyday yearly rates, and it divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12, so it is easy to use in your head.
Keep as a rule [the number] 72 in mind, which you will always divide by the interest, and what results, in that many years it will be doubled.
slides.attribution: Luca Pacioli, Summa de arithmetica (1494), English translation

slides.heading: It works for halving too
slides.text: Divide by the inflation rate instead, and you get roughly how long money takes to lose half its buying power: at 3.5% inflation, about 20 years.

slides.question: Why is the rule usually 72, when 69.3 is more exact for continuous interest?
slides.explanation: 72 is close to the exact answer for everyday yearly rates and splits evenly by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12. Pacioli did not invent it: the rule is thought to be older than his book.
